patients.summary: Forty-year-old international business development manager with bipolar disorder on lithium and stage 3a CKD who joins in 2021. Lithium-era nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is found in 2024, then ciguatera on vacation, saline-induced hyperchloremic acidosis during home IV hydration in 2025, and Ebola virus disease after a 2026 work trip to Guinea, from which he recovers.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: outside primary care
documents.body:
Summary of care, prior primary care office, sent at patient request ahead of transfer.

Patient: Dale Bradley, DOB 04/05/1981.

Problems:
1. Bipolar disorder. Lithium started 2019 by his psychiatrist at the time. Mood has been stable on it and he has had no episodes since. Once he was stable the psychiatrist handed prescribing back to us; we have refilled it since.
2. Chronic kidney disease. Creatinine 1.6 in 2020, 1.7 in spring 2021. eGFR around 50. No proteinuria on prior UA.
3. S/p appendectomy at 18.

Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg capsule, 1 cap twice a day.
Allergies: NKDA.
Immunizations: COVID-19 Pfizer x2, April 2021. Tdap date not on file.
Family hx: father bipolar disorder; mother hypertension.
Social: never smoker, a few drinks a week, works in international business development.

Last lithium level 0.7 (spring 2021). TSH and calcium normal at that draw.

events.reason: New patient, establish care and physical

documents.title: New Patient Visit and Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
New patient. 40M moving his care here after relocating to Haydenville. Records from his prior office reviewed before today.

He is here mostly to get established. Feels well. Works in international business development, on the road abroad several times a year. Sleeps fine, exercises a few times a week.

Bipolar disorder: on lithium since 2019, started by a psychiatrist; prior PCP had been refilling. Mood steady, no highs or lows he can remember in the last two years, no thoughts of self-harm. Takes it twice a day with meals and rarely misses. Happy to keep labs here.

Kidneys: knows he has 'reduced kidney function' — creatinine 1.6-1.7 on outside labs. No swelling, no urinary complaints.

PMH: bipolar disorder; CKD stage 3a. PSH: appendectomy at 18.
Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father with bipolar disorder; mother with hypertension.
SH: never smoker, 2-3 drinks a week, no drug use. Single.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: well-appearing, calm, good eye contact, organized thought. HEENT unremarkable. Thyroid not enlarged. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, old RLQ scar. No edema. No tremor at rest or with arms outstretched. Skin clear.

A/P
1. Bipolar disorder, stable on lithium — continue 300 mg BID. Lithium level, TSH, calcium today, then every 6 months with kidney labs. PHQ-9 2.
2. CKD 3a — CMP, UA, urine albumin/creatinine. Avoid NSAIDs; told him why.
3. Health maintenance — lipids, A1c, one-time HIV and hep C screens. Tdap today (no date on file). COVID primary series done in April. Flu shot in the fall.

RTC 6 months for labs, 1 year for physical.

documents.title: Immunization
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Tdap 0.5 mL IM left deltoid. VIS given. Pt tolerated well, no reaction after 15 minutes.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Dale,

Your labs from Tuesday are in. Lithium level is in the target range. Kidney function is about where your old office had it (creatinine 1.7) — stable, and there's no protein in the urine, which is good. Thyroid, calcium, blood count, sugar and cholesterol all normal. HIV and hepatitis C screens negative.

No changes. We'll repeat the lithium and kidney labs in about six months.

— your primary care physician

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual. Doing well. Busy year — trips to Europe and Asia, no illness on the road. Mood even; sleeping 7 hours. Lithium BID without missed doses. No tremor, no thirst or urinary change, no GI upset.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID. NKDA.
SH unchanged: never smoker, 2-3 drinks/week.

Exam: NAD. HEENT normal. Neck no thyromegaly. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, nontender. No edema. Neuro nonfocal, no tremor. Affect bright, appropriate.

PHQ-9 1.

A/P
- Bipolar disorder: stable. Continue lithium; level and TSH today.
- CKD 3a: CMP, UA, urine albumin/creatinine. Remains off NSAIDs.
- Prevention: hepatitis B series — Heplisav dose 1 today, dose 2 in a month with flu shot. Lipids today. Colon screening starts at 45.

RTC 1 year; labs again in about 6 months.

documents.author: PCP

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit — Thirst and Urination
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 42M on lithium for bipolar disorder (about 5 years now) with CKD 3a. For the past several months he has been thirsty all the time and urinating far more, and it keeps getting worse. Up three or four times a night to void. Tired during the day even though he gets enough sleep. Drinking roughly 4-5 L of water a day; keeps a bottle on his desk at work because if he goes without he gets lightheaded and his mouth goes dry. No travel lately, no vomiting or diarrhea. Mood stable, no change in lithium dose or timing, no new meds or supplements.

O: T 36.7, BP 124/78, P 76. BMI 23. Alert, oriented, conversational, no change in mentation. Mucous membranes a little dry. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No edema. No tremor. Exam otherwise unremarkable.

A/P: Polyuria and polydipsia on long-term lithium. Need to sort out water diuresis versus solute (glucose, calcium) and kidney-concentrating defect.
- BMP (sodium, glucose, calcium, creatinine), serum osmolality, urine osmolality, lithium level today.
- Do not restrict fluids at home — drink to thirst.
- Will call with results; if the picture fits, a desmopressin trial here in the office later this week.

Patient agrees.

documents.title: Results — osmolality
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt. Serum osm 302 with Na 145 — concentrated blood — while urine osm only 148, i.e., dilute urine despite that. Glucose and calcium normal; lithium 0.8; creatinine at his usual. Picture is a concentrating defect. Explained plan for desmopressin trial Thursday morning: come in having drunk normally, we'll check urine before and two hours after a small injection. He'll come at 8.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Desmopressin Trial
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt arrived 0800, drank normally overnight. Baseline urine collected 0805. Desmopressin 2 mcg SC L abdomen at 0812 per PCP order. Pt allowed water to thirst. Voided 0910 (large volume) and second sample collected 1010. VS stable throughout. No headache or nausea. Pt to wait for PCP call this afternoon.

documents.title: Desmopressin Trial — Result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Urine osm 152 before desmopressin and 163 two hours after — essentially no response, against a serum osm of 302 on Monday. That is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Spoke with him by phone. He understands his kidneys aren't responding to the water-holding hormone and that the thirst is protective: never restrict his own water, keep fluids with him when traveling, and call early with any vomiting or diarrhea since he can dry out fast.

Plan: continue lithium 300 mg BID unchanged. NDI added to problem list. Sodium and kidney labs with his usual lithium checks.

events.reason: Vomiting, diarrhea and tingling after a fish meal

medications.sig: Dissolve 1 tablet on the tongue every 8 hours as needed for nausea

documents.title: Emergency Department Record (outside, received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Received by fax 06/28/2024 at patient request. Emergency department, Nassau, Bahamas. Date of service 06/19/2024.

Visitor, 43-year-old man on holiday. About three hours after a dinner of grilled reef fish at a seaside restaurant he developed nausea, repeated vomiting and loose stools. Gut symptoms came first; over the next few hours his hands and feet began to tingle ('pins and needles') and he noticed cold water felt hot on his skin and a warm cup felt cold. No fever. Has only been in the Caribbean. His companion had a different meal and is well.

PMH (per patient): bipolar disorder on lithium; chronic kidney disease; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Appendectomy. Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily. Allergies: none known.

Vitals stable on arrival and at discharge.
Exam: alert and oriented, mildly dry. Cranial nerves intact. Strength 5/5 throughout. Light touch reduced in a stocking-and-glove pattern. No rash. No rigidity. Abdomen soft, nontender.

Labs: CBC normal. Electrolytes normal. Creatinine elevated, consistent with his known kidney disease.

Impression: ciguatera fish poisoning.

ED course: IV fluids 1 L, ondansetron 4 mg IV with relief of nausea. Tolerating fluids by mouth at discharge.

Discharge: ondansetron 4 mg ODT q8h prn. No fish or alcohol for the next several months — they can bring symptoms back. Tingling and temperature reversal may last weeks. See your own doctor when home. Return for weakness, trouble breathing, fainting or a slow pulse.

documents.title: Food poisoning on vacation
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Back from the Bahamas. Last Wednesday I got sick a few hours after eating fish — throwing up, diarrhea — and ended up in the ER there. They said ciguatera. Stomach is fine now but my hands and feet still tingle and cold things feel hot, which is bizarre. Do I need to be seen? I'm keeping up with water.

documents.title: RE: Food poisoning on vacation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Glad you're home. Yes, I'd like to see you — let's do Wednesday. With the vomiting and your kidneys I also want to check your sodium and lithium level. If you can get the ER paperwork sent to us, please do. In the meantime keep drinking, and skip alcohol.

events.reason: Follow-up after ED visit for ciguatera

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-ED Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen in an emergency department in the Bahamas 6/19 — GI illness starting about 3 h after grilled fish, then distal paresthesias and hot/cold reversal. Told ciguatera; got IV fluids and ondansetron. Paperwork not here yet.

Now: vomiting and diarrhea stopped by the next morning. Used two ondansetron tabs, none since Friday. Still has tingling in fingers and soles, and cold drinks feel 'spicy-hot' in his mouth, but both a little less each day. No weakness, no palpitations, no dizziness. Drinking his usual large volumes. Has not had alcohol or fish since.

Meds: lithium 300 mg BID (never stopped). NKDA.

Exam: well, hydrated. HR regular. CN intact. Strength full, reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Light touch decreased in stocking-glove distribution; vibration and position sense preserved. Gait normal.

A/P
1. Ciguatera fish poisoning with persistent sensory symptoms — expected to fade over weeks. Avoid fish and alcohol for a few months. No specific treatment. Call if weakness or worsening.
2. NDI / CKD 3a / lithium, after a few days of GI losses — BMP and lithium level today.

Check in by phone in about 6 weeks.

documents.title: Labs from yesterday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Sodium and potassium normal, kidney numbers right at your usual, lithium level 0.8 — no harm done from the vomiting. Keep up the fluids, and let the tingling settle on its own.

documents.title: Phone follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Planned call. Tingling much better — only notices it now and then in his toes. Cold drinks still feel a bit odd occasionally. No weakness. Has stayed off fish and alcohol. Reassured; will reassess at his September physical.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual exam, 43M.

Interval: NDI diagnosed in March by desmopressin trial; drinks to thirst, nocturia twice nightly, which he has made peace with. Ciguatera in June — tingling and temperature reversal fully gone since late August. Back to eating fish occasionally and his usual couple of drinks, without any return of symptoms. Mood steady. PHQ-9 2.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID. NKDA.

Exam: well-appearing. Vitals reviewed. HEENT normal, moist mucosa. Neck supple, thyroid normal. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No edema. Neuro: strength, reflexes, light touch and vibration normal in all four limbs. No tremor.

A/P
- Ciguatera poisoning — resolved; off the active list.
- NDI, CKD 3a, bipolar disorder on lithium — CMP, lithium level, TSH, UA, urine albumin/creatinine. Same lithium dose.
- Prevention — lipids today; flu and COVID at a nurse visit in October. Colon cancer screening at 45 — we'll set it up next year.

RTC 1 year; labs around February.

documents.title: Lab review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Creatinine at his baseline, Na normal, lithium therapeutic, TSH normal, UA dilute but otherwise clean, urine albumin normal, lipids fine. Message to pt.

documents.title: Nurse Visit — Vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Late-day vaccine visit after work. Influenza trivalent 0.5 mL IM left arm; Pfizer 2024-25 COVID 0.3 mL IM right arm. Screening questions negative. Watched 15 min, no problems.

documents.title: Lab review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Lithium therapeutic. Na normal. Creatinine unchanged. Will go over in person at his March visit.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Chronic Care Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Six-month check on his chronic issues. February labs reviewed with him: creatinine at baseline, lithium in range, sodium normal.

NDI: still drinking a lot, up twice a night; no dizzy spells since he started keeping water with him everywhere. Bipolar disorder: steady, nothing to report. Uses Tylenol only. Traveling less this quarter.

Exam: well. Mucous membranes moist. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema, no tremor.

A/P
- CKD 3a: stable. NSAID avoidance reinforced.
- NDI: drink to thirst; call early with any GI illness.
- Bipolar disorder on lithium 300 mg BID: continue; next labs with the October physical.

RTC October.

orders.reason: dehydration from gastroenteritis with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

documents.title: Video Visit — Vomiting and Diarrhea
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, pt at home. Called this morning.

Since Sunday night: vomiting several times a day and watery diarrhea, maybe 6-8 times a day. No blood, no fever he's measured. Can keep down sips but with his NDI he's still urinating large amounts and can't drink enough to keep up. Lightheaded when he stands. Mouth dry. Last void dilute as always.

On video: tired-appearing, lips dry, speaking full sentences, oriented.

A/P: Viral gastroenteritis with dehydration in a man with nephrogenic DI who loses free water continuously — high risk of getting behind.
- Home IV hydration through home infusion agency: normal saline 1 L over 2 h twice daily x 5 days. Agency to place a peripheral IV this afternoon.
- Ondansetron 4 mg ODT q8h prn so he can drink.
- Keep taking lithium.
- Call if he can't keep anything down, has fainting, confusion or blood in stool.

documents.title: Home infusion nurse report
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Home infusion RN called: 22g PIV placed L forearm yesterday afternoon, first liter in without problem, second at bedtime. Pt still with loose stools but vomiting less, took ondansetron x2. Agency visiting daily. Will call with concerns.

conditions.label: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to excess normal saline infusion

documents.title: Emergency Department Record (outside, received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Date of service 06/23/2025. Copy to primary care.

CC: weak and worn out x 2 days.

HPI: 44M with CKD, bipolar disorder on lithium and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Developed a stomach bug about a week ago; his PCP arranged home IV fluids for dehydration, which he has been getting twice a day through a home infusion service. GI symptoms are much better, but for two days he has felt profoundly weak and fatigued. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no fever.

History per patient and prior records: CKD; bipolar disorder; nephrogenic DI; ciguatera poisoning last year. Appendectomy. Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID; normal saline 1 L IV BID at home; ondansetron prn. NKDA.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 88, afebrile. Comfortable. Mucous membranes moist, skin turgor normal. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. Neuro nonfocal.

Labs: Na 140, K 3.9, Cl 115, HCO3 18, BUN 29, Cr 2.1, glucose 98. ABG pH 7.32 / pCO2 40 / pO2 98.

MDM: Normal anion gap acidosis with chloride 115 after several days of large-volume normal saline. Volume status now replete. Picture fits hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from excess saline.

Plan: home saline discontinued — agency notified; peripheral IV removed here. Oral fluids encouraged, tolerated well in the department. Discharged home. Follow up with PCP within 2-3 days for repeat chemistry. Return for worsening weakness, confusion, or inability to drink.

Dx: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to excess normal saline infusion.

documents.title: Home infusion agency
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Home infusion agency called: ED notified them yesterday to stop the saline; IV was pulled in the ED. Remaining bags picked up this morning. Orders closed on their end. Pt has follow-up here Thursday.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen in the ED Monday for weakness after five days of home normal saline — chloride 115, bicarb 18, pH 7.32, creatinine 2.1. Diagnosed with hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from the saline; infusions stopped.

Today: energy coming back. No vomiting since last Thursday, stools formed since the weekend. Eating normally, drinking his usual large volumes by mouth. No dizziness standing. Taking lithium as usual. No ondansetron since Saturday.

Exam: looks well. Moist mucosa. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abd soft, nontender. Former IV site L forearm clean, no cord or redness.

A/P
1. Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis — repeat BMP today.
2. Gastroenteritis and dehydration — resolved.
3. CKD 3a / NDI / lithium — creatinine on today's panel; lithium level with the next routine set.

Repeat BMP in two weeks.

documents.title: Yesterday's labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Better already: chloride down to 109 and bicarbonate up to 22 (from 115 and 18 in the ED). Creatinine 1.9, coming back toward your usual. Keep drinking normally — no extra salt tablets or sports-drink loading needed. Recheck on the 10th.

conditions.label: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to excess normal saline infusion

documents.title: Lab review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Cl 104, HCO3 25, Cr 1.7 — acidosis resolved, kidney function back to baseline. Problem resolved. Pt messaged.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
44M, yearly exam.

Interval: June gastroenteritis treated with home IV saline, then ED visit for hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis — resolved by the July recheck. Feels fully himself since. Mood stable; PHQ-9 1. NDI unchanged, drinking to thirst. Expects to be traveling more again next year.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID. NKDA.
SH: never smoker; 2-3 drinks/wk.

Exam: well-appearing. HEENT normal. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. Neuro nonfocal. No tremor. Skin without lesions of concern.

A/P
- CKD 3a, NDI, bipolar disorder on lithium: CMP, lithium level, TSH, UA, urine albumin/creatinine today. No change.
- Colorectal cancer screening: turns 45 in April. Prefers stool testing to colonoscopy — FIT kit to go out in the spring.
- Lipids today. Flu and COVID at a nurse visit later this month.

RTC 1 year; labs in January.

events.reason: Fever after travel to West Africa

documents.title: After-hours call — fever after travel
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt called my cell early Saturday. Back one week from a month in Guinea for work. Two days of fever, achy, sore throat; since last night vomiting and watery diarrhea, crampy belly pain. Volunteered that he helped a family prepare a body for a funeral while he was there.

Told him not to come to the office or urgent care and not to take a rideshare. Spoke with the regional hospital ED attending, who will receive him through their isolation entrance; ambulance arranged with notice to EMS. Called the state public health epidemiology line; they will coordinate with the hospital. Pt understands and is staying in his own room until transport.

events.reason: Fever, vomiting, diarrhea after travel to Guinea

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Admission History and Physical (outside, received)
documents.author: infectious disease
documents.body:
Regional hospital, biocontainment intensive care unit. Admission 06/20/2026. Sent to primary care at their request.

Reason for admission: fever and GI illness after travel to Guinea, with high-risk exposure.

HPI: 45-year-old man (CKD, bipolar disorder on lithium carbonate, nephrogenic DI; past ciguatera poisoning and saline-related hyperchloremic acidosis) came home to the US a week ago from a month of business travel in Guinea, in both cities and rural districts. While there he went to a funeral, had close contact with relatives of the person who died and helped wash and prepare the body. Now with fever, diffuse abdominal pain and many episodes of non-bloody emesis and watery stool, plus myalgias, malaise and sore throat. He did not eat undercooked meat and did not swim or wade in fresh water. His PCP and public health were in contact before arrival; he came by EMS directly into isolation.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID. Allergies: NKDA. Never smoker, social alcohol.

Exam: T 39.2 C, HR 110, BP 96/64, RR 22. Acutely ill, dry. Conjunctivae injected. Posterior pharynx mildly red. Heart tachycardic, regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen tender throughout, no rebound, no guarding. No rash, no petechiae, no bleeding from any site. Alert, no focal deficit.

Initial labs: WBC 3.1, platelets 82, AST 286, ALT 174, creatinine 2.4. Malaria rapid antigen negative, thick and thin smears without parasites. Blood cultures sent.

Assessment: suspected viral hemorrhagic fever given the funeral exposure. Full biocontainment precautions. Supportive care started while confirmatory testing is run with the state laboratory.

Addendum 06/21: Ebola virus RT-PCR on blood DETECTED (Zaire). Ansuvimab given as a single infusion today. Lithium held while volume status and kidney function are unstable. Public health notified; contact tracing under way.

documents.title: Discharge Summary (outside, received)
documents.author: infectious disease
documents.body:
Regional hospital — biocontainment ICU, Infectious Disease service.
Admitted 06/20/2026. Discharged 07/09/2026.

Principal diagnosis: Ebola virus disease (Zaire ebolavirus), confirmed by blood RT-PCR 06/21.
Other problems: chronic kidney disease; bipolar disorder on lithium; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; history of ciguatera poisoning.

Course: Presented febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive with vomiting and diarrhea after funeral exposure in Guinea. Malaria testing negative; blood cultures no growth. Received ansuvimab 50 mg/kg IV once on 06/21. Supportive care with IV balanced crystalloid (chosen over saline given his prior saline-related acidosis), electrolyte replacement and antiemetics; strict intake/output given his NDI. Lithium held from admission. GI losses slowed over the first week; fever resolved by 06/28. Thrombocytopenia, leukopenia and transaminase elevation improved steadily without bleeding. Creatinine 2.4 on arrival, 1.8 at discharge. Blood RT-PCR not detected 07/06 and 07/08; released from isolation by the infection prevention team and public health.

Discharge labs (07/08): WBC 5.4, platelets 206, AST 44, ALT 61, creatinine 1.8.
Discharge vitals: T 36.8, HR 78, BP 118/74, RR 16.

Discharge medications: RESUME lithium carbonate 300 mg BID.

Survivor instructions: Use condoms for every sexual contact for at least 12 months from illness onset or until two semen tests are negative. Semen testing through our ID survivor clinic, starting about three months from onset. Eye exam with ophthalmology in the coming weeks. Report eye pain, redness or vision change promptly.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week (lithium level and chemistry); ID survivor clinic in about one month.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit. Discharge summary reviewed in full.

Admitted 6/20-7/9 to the regional hospital's biocontainment ICU with Ebola virus disease after funeral exposure in Guinea; ansuvimab 6/21, supportive care, lithium held. Two negative blood PCRs before discharge.

Since home: tired, napping most afternoons, but better each day. No fever. Appetite returning, stools normal. Drinking well. Back on lithium since 7/9 — mood steady through all of this, he says, more worn out than low.

Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg BID. NKDA.

Exam: well-appearing, a little tired. Afebrile. Conjunctivae clear. Pharynx normal. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. No rash. Neuro nonfocal, no tremor.

A/P
1. Ebola virus disease, recovering — CBC and CMP today to confirm counts and liver tests keep improving. Reinforced: condoms with any sexual contact for at least 12 months from onset or until two negative semen tests; ID survivor clinic will run semen testing. Ophthalmology referral placed for the survivor eye exam; call right away for eye pain, redness or blurred vision.
2. Lithium resumed — level today (5 days on), plus creatinine. CKD 3a: creatinine 1.8 at discharge.
3. NDI — continue to drink to thirst.

Recheck mid-September.

documents.title: Your labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good news across the board: white count, platelets and liver tests are all normal now. Creatinine is 1.8, close to your usual. Lithium level is 0.6 — on the low side of our range, which is fine while you're getting back on your feet; we'll recheck in September. Eye appointment request has gone to ophthalmology.

documents.title: Ophthalmology Letter (outside, received)
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Outside ophthalmology practice. Date of visit 08/05/2026.

Thank you for sending Mr. Bradley, a 45-year-old man seen for a screening examination about seven weeks after Ebola virus disease. He has no eye pain, redness, floaters, light sensitivity or change in vision.

Visual acuity 20/20 in each eye uncorrected. Pupils equal and reactive, no afferent defect. Intraocular pressures normal. Slit lamp: lids and conjunctivae quiet, corneas clear, anterior chambers deep and quiet without cell or flare, lenses clear. Dilated fundus exam: vitreous clear, discs sharp with healthy rims, maculae and vessels normal, peripheral retina flat without lesions, both eyes.

Impression: normal eye examination; no evidence of uveitis.

Plan: no treatment. He should return promptly for any eye pain, redness or blurring. Routine follow-up otherwise.

Ophthalmology

documents.title: ID Survivor Clinic Letter (outside, received)
documents.author: infectious disease
documents.body:
Infectious Disease survivor clinic, regional hospital. Visit date 08/12/2026.

Mr. Bradley returns about one month after discharge from our biocontainment unit for Ebola virus disease (onset mid-June 2026). He reports his energy is coming back steadily; he is working from home full days and walking daily. No fevers, eye symptoms, hearing change or new joint complaints. Back on lithium without trouble. Normal eye exam with ophthalmology last week reviewed. Your July labs reviewed.

Exam today unremarkable.

Plan:
- Semen Ebola RNA testing to begin at three months from onset, in September 2026, then monthly until two consecutive negatives.
- Continue condom use with any sexual contact until then, and for at least 12 months from onset.
- Return to our clinic after the first semen result.

Thank you for allowing us to share in his care.
Infectious Disease

documents.body: Quick update — saw the eye doctor and the ID clinic, both fine. Energy is maybe 80% of normal and better every week. I'm almost through the 90-day supply of lithium from May; can you send a refill to the usual pharmacy?

documents.body: Great to hear, and I've read both letters. Refill sent — same dose, 300 mg twice a day. See you on September 16th; we'll recheck the lithium level and kidney labs that morning.
